rationale: Grammatical inverse: A 'Windows NT descendant of Windows 2000' and B 'Windows 2000 has descendant Windows NT' are the same assertion, but the paragraph's wording ('Windows NT (and its descendants, Windows 2000...)') supports only the reversed NT-as-ancestor direction; the inverse relation is equivalent regardless.

Same subject, object, and dates (20 June–20 July 1861 vs June 20–July 20 1861). Relation 'first commander' and 'commander of' are inverse/synonymous and the start/end qualifiers match; entity type labels differ only in wording.

B adds the qualifier 'almost exclusively' (approximation), which A lacks. The paragraph says Unicode is used 'almost exclusively' for new systems, so B is a qualified claim that A does not make; not the same complete assertion.

Same subject and object with same relation 'cares for'. Frequency qualifiers 'from time to time' and 'occasionally' are synonymous in meaning. Entity type labels (human vs fictional character) differ, but both refer to the same fictional character subject and object.

Same subject, relation 'position held', dates (Jan 10 2011–Jan 14 2013), and electoral district 5. Object labels 'Arizona House of Representatives' and 'member of the Arizona House of Representatives' denote the same position.
Same subject, object, relation, and date (July 21 1861). B adds a 'description: first major engagement' qualifier not present in A; B is narrower/more specific than A, so not equivalent.
Same subject, object, and relation. B adds a 'purpose: internal character encoding' qualifier absent in A; the extra qualifier makes B a narrower claim, so not equivalent.
Identical subject, relation ('date of birth'), object (June 19, 1946), and no qualifiers in either.
Same subject and object (United States); relations 'country of citizenship' and 'nationality' are synonymous, and neither has qualifiers.
Grammatical inverse of 'descendant of' / 'has descendant' between Windows NT and Windows XP; the paragraph lists XP among NT's descendants. The inverse pair is the same assertion.
Identical subject, object, relation 'exempt from', and condition qualifier. Both are the same assertion.

Same subject, object, relation, and dates/district. The end-date qualifier label differs ('point in time end' vs 'point in time') but both denote the same end date of January 14, 2013 in the same role.

Same value 110 light-years, but B adds an 'approximately' approximation qualifier that A does not have. A states the distance without hedging, so the two differ in qualification and are not equivalent.

Same subject, object (Beauregard), and relation 'first commander' for the Army of Northern Virginia with the same period June 20–July 20, 1861. A uses start/end qualifiers and B a single point-in-time range; the content is the same. Subject type labels differ only in wording.
Grammatical inverse: A 'First Corps joined by Army of the Shenandoah' and B 'Army of the Shenandoah joined First Corps' express the same event on 20 July 1861 as stated in the paragraph.

Same subject, object ('protocol'), and relation 'added as'. B adds a point-in-time qualifier 1992 absent in A. The paragraph supports the year, but A does not express it, so B is a more specific assertion and not equivalent.

Same object and relation. A has a purpose qualifier ('aims of Agreement on Social Policy') that B omits, so B is broader and missing a meaningful condition/qualifier. Subject type label differences do not matter.
Same subject HD 11964 c and same object HD 11964; 'orbits' and 'host star' are synonymous for the planet-star relation, with no qualifiers in either.
Same year 2005 and subject. A carries a 'possible' discovery-status qualifier that B omits, so A is qualified (uncertain discovery) and B is an unqualified assertion. Not equivalent.
Same creator and flag. A has a time qualifier 'June-July 1861' absent in B, so B is less specified and the two are not the same complete assertion.

Inverse pair (commander of / commanded by) between Beauregard and First Corps, but A carries an 'under: General J.E. Johnston' qualifier that B omits. A's qualifier is a meaningful condition, so the assertions are not equivalent.

A asserts Protocol part of Maastricht Treaty with negative polarity; B asserts protocol 'is not a chapter of' Maastricht Treaty. Both carry the same negative polarity; the relation wording differs in phrasing but the negated membership claim is the same.

Same subject (Social Charter) and relation 'adopted by'. A's object '11 of the then 12 member states' and B's 'member states' with count 11 of 12 denote the same group; B merely restates the count as a qualifier.
Same subject HD 11964 c, relation 'minimum mass', and value 35 Earth masses. B adds a unit qualifier 'Earth mass' which restates the unit already contained in A's object, so no meaningful difference.
